why: The best browsing hour in Tokyo for two of your threads at once: antiquarian shops selling original ukiyo-e woodblock prints and Edo maps, and art-and-photobook dealers stacked four floors high. Ten minutes west of the Ochanomizu instrument street, so it closes out the Akihabara walk. Caution: a good number of the shops shut on Sundays, some on Mondays, and most close around 18:00, so get there before 17:00.

name: TAIKO-LAB Aoyama
what: Dedicated taiko school offering a 60-minute English-language hands-on Japanese drumming experience.
why: Very easy to integrate into a Tokyo trip: professional instruction, drums and sticks are provided, beginners are welcome regardless of age, and the session builds toward playing a complete piece before an instructor performs a taiko solo.

name: Oedo Sukeroku Taiko Dojo
what: Private and small-group taiko lessons taught in English or Japanese by professional Oedo Sukeroku Taiko players.
why: A more traditional and serious alternative to a packaged visitor experience. The dojo explicitly offers 1- and 1.5-hour lessons for travelers and families, including complete beginners, and lets you learn directly from professional performers in the influential Oedo Sukeroku taiko tradition.

name: HIBIKUS Asakusa Basement
what: Taiko school and workshop studio beneath the headquarters of historic Japanese drum maker Miyamoto Unosuke Shoten.
why: BOOKED — this is the taiko lesson for the trip, chosen for being in the neighborhood: a real taiko school rather than a tourist attraction, professional players teaching, students from age three up, and a five-minute walk from the hotel so the lesson morning starts without a train. The basement studio is a historic space once used to store mikoshi and later as an air-raid shelter. Confirm they will run a single visitor session on Mon 19 Oct.

name: Taikokan Drum Museum
what: Small specialist museum created by Miyamoto Unosuke Shoten with hundreds of Japanese and international drums, including instruments visitors can actually play.
why: A particularly good companion to a taiko lesson for a drummer: the collection contains roughly 800 drums, selected exhibits marked with a musical-note symbol can be played, and the Miyamoto Unosuke shop downstairs sells taiko, bachi and other traditional percussion equipment.
mapQuery: Taikokan Drum Museum Miyamoto Unosuke 2-1-1 Nishiasakusa Tokyo

name: ZAKURO SHOW — October 23, 2026
what: October 23, 2026 bilingual one-hour live concert featuring taiko alongside koto, shamisen, shakuhachi and other traditional Japanese instruments.
why: Confirmed for October 23 during the Tokyo trip. It is an intimate performance with top-level traditional musicians only a few feet from the audience, with English explanations of the instruments and music. This is broader than a pure taiko concert but provides a strong live-performance counterpart to a hands-on taiko lesson.

name: Nakamise-dori
what: Historic shopping street running from Kaminarimon toward Senso-ji, lined with traditional snacks, souvenirs and small shops.
why: Several of the recommended ryokan sit immediately beside it, making the historic commercial streetscape part of the everyday experience rather than a separate sightseeing excursion.

name: Kaminarimon
what: The iconic Thunder Gate marking the entrance to Senso-ji and Nakamise-dori.
why: One of the defining landmarks of the neighborhood and immediately accessible from several of the small hotels and ryokan considered for the trip.

name: Traditional Asakusa Ryokan & Futon Stay
what: Spend one or more Tokyo nights in a tatami room sleeping on traditional Japanese futon bedding.
why: The useful compromise is choosing a traditional room with a private Western-style toilet and bathroom rather than sacrificing basic convenience purely for authenticity.

name: Hakone Overnight Trip
what: Potential one-night excursion from Tokyo to Hakone for mountain scenery and a traditional ryokan experience.
why: Discussed as a better place than central Tokyo to spend money on one special traditional ryokan night. It would create a clear contrast with a simple Asakusa base.

name: Private Family Onsen / Kashikiri-buro
what: A reservable private hot-spring bath used only by your party for a scheduled period.
why: Discussed as an alternative to gender-separated public bathing for a father traveling with a 13-year-old daughter. It removes the need for either traveler to enter a public bath alone.

name: Ryokan with Private In-Room Onsen
what: Traditional ryokan room with its own private hot-spring bath, sometimes outdoors on a terrace.
why: Discussed as the easiest onsen arrangement for an adult father and 13-year-old daughter because each person can use the bath privately at different times while still getting the full ryokan experience.

name: Sokichi Kiriko Experience Workshop
what: Hands-on Edo Kiriko workshop where you use a grinding wheel to cut traditional geometric patterns into your own glass.
why: One of the strongest craft choices for the trip because you actually work with the cutting equipment rather than simply decorate a souvenir. Sokichi's official workshop allows participants age 9+, so a 13-year-old is explicitly eligible, and beginner patterns and English-language information are available.

name: Sumida Edo Kiriko-kan
what: Working Edo Kiriko studio, shop and small exhibition where visitors can reserve a traditional glass-cutting experience.
why: A more workshop-oriented alternative to Sokichi where you can see professional Edo Kiriko work and then cut a glass yourself. The official site accepts workshop participants from elementary-school fourth grade, so a 13-year-old is suitable.
mapQuery: Sumida Edo Kiriko-kan 2-10-9 Taihei Sumida Tokyo

name: watashino Washi Papermaking Experience
what: Hands-on workshop where you form traditional Japanese washi paper and make four postcard-sized sheets to take home.
why: Unlike a paper-decorating activity, you actually perform the sheet-forming part of papermaking. It is compact enough to combine with an Asakusa day and is particularly good if you both enjoy materials, paper, drawing or printing.

name: Ozu Washi
what: Historic washi specialist founded in 1653 with a shop, museum, gallery and hands-on studio for making a sheet of Japanese paper.
why: The deeper and more historically focused washi option: you can make an A4 sheet with traditional tools, then examine regional papers and the history of the material. Particularly interesting for someone interested in art materials and fabrication rather than just souvenirs.

name: Kumihimo Experience by DOMYO
what: Traditional silk-cord braiding workshop using authentic kumihimo equipment at a braiding house founded in 1652.
why: One of the least touristy and most technically interesting choices discussed. You learn the history of kumihimo and braid a strap or bracelet from silk thread using the same basic tools and processes associated with traditional Japanese cord making. English-language workshop plans are offered.
mapQuery: Kumihimo Experience by DOMYO 6-75 Kagurazaka Tokyo

name: Aizome Museum
what: Small working indigo-dyeing museum and studio where a traditional craftsman offers reservation-only tenugui indigo-dyeing experiences.
why: A particularly authentic option: this is a working Sumida craft studio rather than a generic tourist class. You can see traditional indigo-dyed yukata, hanten, carved stencils and tools and arrange a hands-on tenugui dyeing experience. The workshop actively teaches indigo dyeing to school groups, making it a strong candidate for a 13-year-old, though no specific minimum age was found.

name: somenova
what: Dyeing workshop operated by Miyakozome's dye manufacturer, whose business dates to 1890, offering hands-on Japanese textile-dyeing experiences.
why: A more structured and accessible alternative to the tiny Aizome Museum, with multiple dyeing techniques and projects. A current furoshiki shibori-style dyeing workshop is scheduled through January 2027; a third-party booking source lists it as unsuitable only for children under 5, so age 13 is appropriate for that specific program.

name: Tsukada Kobo
what: Seventh-generation Edo kimekomi doll workshop where visitors can learn the traditional technique of pressing patterned fabric into precisely cut grooves.
why: Founded in 1841 and still a working doll atelier. We discussed its newer sumo-wrestler experience as especially fun because it combines a serious traditional technique with an amusing object to take home; the studio also offers traditional owl kimekomi workshops. No specific minimum age was confirmed.

name: Tanaka Sudare
what: Meiji-era Edo sudare workshop where visitors can watch traditional bamboo-blind production and weave a coaster, mat or other small sudare piece.
why: One of the most appealing options if you want an actual working craftsman's shop rather than a polished tourist workshop. You manipulate the bamboo and weighted weaving tools yourself and leave with the object you made. The studio explicitly accepts educational visits by children and a current booking listing allows participants from age 6, so age 13 is suitable.

name: Tsumami-zaiku / Kanzashi Workshop
what: Traditional craft experience folding and pinching tiny squares of fabric into flowers used for Japanese kanzashi hair ornaments.
why: Fine, precise handwork that seemed particularly appropriate for a capable 13-year-old: the technique uses tweezers to transform small fabric pieces into surprisingly elaborate floral forms. We discussed the craft and Asakusabashi as the place to look for it, but did not identify a specific verified workshop operator, so the location remains area-level.

name: Kintsugi Tsugu Tsugu Ebisu Studio
what: Dedicated kintsugi studio teaching Japanese techniques for visibly repairing broken ceramics with lacquer and metallic finishes.
why: Conceptually one of the most interesting crafts discussed because the repair becomes part of the object's design. Tsugu Tsugu teaches both traditional urushi-based kintsugi and shorter kintsugi-style experiences. We noted that tourist kintsugi classes vary substantially in authenticity, so the specific course should be checked before booking. No minimum age for the relevant October workshop was confirmed.

name: Edo Taito Traditional Crafts Center
what: Free traditional-crafts center displaying hundreds of examples of Tokyo handicrafts, with regular artisan demonstrations and occasional hands-on programs.
why: Useful as the overview stop for the entire craft theme, especially if staying in Asakusa. It lets you see dozens of craft traditions before or after doing one yourself, and weekend demonstrations provide a chance to watch working craftspeople rather than only finished objects.
mapQuery: Edo Taito Traditional Crafts Center 2-22-13 Asakusa Tokyo

what: THE SIXTH LIE live at Harajuku RUIDO on Oct. 23, 2026.
why: Electronic/cinematic Japanese rock in a small venue; the event explicitly permits school-age children, so a 13-year-old can attend.

name: Yanaka Ginza
what: Traditional shopping street famous for its resident cats, cat-themed shops, and old-Tokyo atmosphere.
why: The cat neighborhood — stray cats lounging on rooftops, cat sculptures, cat-shaped snacks. Pairs perfectly with nearby Nezu Shrine for a quiet Yanaka half-day.

name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building
what: Free observation decks at 202m in Tange's iconic twin towers, with panoramic views of Tokyo and Mt. Fuji on clear days.
why: The free alternative to paid observation decks — same height as Shibuya Sky, zero cost. Best at sunset or after dark. October has good Fuji visibility odds.

name: Momotaro Jeans Aoyama
what: Flagship store for Momotaro's premium Japanese selvedge denim, known for the peach logo and Zimbabwe cotton.
why: The flagship experience for one of Japan's top denim brands — proper fitting, full range of cuts, and staff who know raw denim. The pink inseam stitching is iconic.

name: Pure Blue Japan Harajuku
what: Cult Japanese denim brand specializing in slubby, textured selvedge with dramatic fading potential.
why: PBJ's signature XX fabric is some of the most interesting denim made anywhere — heavy slub, electric blue weft, and fades that look hand-painted after a year of wear.

name: Kapital Ebisu
what: Multi-floor flagship for Kapital's patchwork denim, boro-inspired pieces, and Americana-meets-Japan aesthetic. The 2-20-2 Ebisu-minami address (Gaia Ebisu Building) now also appears as the KAPITAL Tokyo Naked Store, 11:00–20:00.
why: Not just jeans — Kapital is a whole world of sashiko stitching, century denim, and pieces that look like they survived a hundred years of wear. The Ebisu store is the full experience.

name: Azabudai Hills Sky Lobby
what: Free 34th-floor Sky Lobby in Tokyo's newest skyscraper (2023), with floor-to-ceiling windows and Tokyo Tower views.
why: Brand new, free, and uncrowded compared to the big-name observation decks. The Tokyo Tower framing is particularly good — it's right there at eye level. Pairs with the teamLab Borderless that moved here.
mapQuery: Azabudai Hills Mori JP Tower Tokyo

why: One of the easiest dedicated capybara experiences to combine with an Asakusa day, with unusually close interaction.

why: The unusual combination of capybaras and cats makes this substantially different from either a normal cat cafe or capybara cafe.

why: A particularly unusual animal interaction and an easy addition to a Kichijoji and Inokashira Park day.

why: Extremely convenient if already exploring Takeshita Street and centered almost entirely on direct capybara interaction.

why: Fennecs are far less commonly encountered than the cats, dogs, pigs, and hedgehogs found at most Tokyo animal cafes.

name: mipig cafe Harajuku

why: The pigs actively interact with visitors and the experience is more hands-on than simply viewing animals.

name: Chiku Chiku Cafe
what: Hedgehog cafe where individual hedgehogs occupy miniature dollhouse-like environments and can be handled.
why: The miniature-room setup makes it considerably more visually distinctive than a standard small-animal cafe.

name: Yadorigi Cafe & Restaurant
what: Cat cafe and restaurant centered around rescue cats rather than the usual purpose-bred cat-cafe format.
why: Combines an actual cafe and meal experience with cats and fits naturally into a walk through Yanaka.

name: pignic cafe Kichijoji
what: Private-room micro-pig cafe beside Inokashira Park, with some sessions offering walks with a pig in the park.
why: The private rooms and seasonal pig-walking experience make it much more unusual than a standard micro-pig cafe.

name: Samoyed Cafe moffu Harajuku
what: Dog cafe devoted specifically to large, fluffy Samoyeds.
why: A room full of Samoyeds is a much more specific and memorable experience than a conventional dog cafe.

name: Torinoirukafe Yanaka Honten
what: Bird cafe specializing in owls and other birds, with close-up viewing and interaction.
why: A useful contrast to mammal cafes and particularly convenient when exploring Yanaka and the Ueno side of Tokyo.

name: Harajuku Kawaii Zoo Land
what: Mixed-animal interaction venue featuring a changing collection that can include capybaras, meerkats, fennecs, ferrets, hedgehogs, and other small animals.
why: One stop provides access to several unusual species instead of specializing in only one animal.

why: The free fallback if Shibuya Sky's sunset slots are gone for 23 Oct — 11F, overlooks Shibuya but not the scramble crossing itself, and no ticket needed.
mapQuery: Shibuya Hikarie Sky Lobby Tokyo Japan

name: Hachiko Commemorative Stamp
what: Eki-stamp at SHIBU HACHI BOX tourist info center near Hachiko statue
why: 2-minute detour on any Shibuya visit; start an eki-stamp collection across the 9 days — bring a small ink pad
mapQuery: SHIBU HACHI BOX Shibuya Station Tokyo Japan

name: Camera no Kitamura - Shinjuku
what: Multi-floor camera shop with junk section and dedicated Leica floor
why: Go for the junk section — that's the actual fun; pairs same-afternoon with Map Camera

name: Lemon-sha Ginza
what: 40-year Ginza camera institution with film cameras, fountain pens, and watches
why: Strong used counter for medium format; pairs naturally with Ginza Tsuboyaki-imo on a Ginza afternoon
mapQuery: Lemon-sha Ginza Church Building Tokyo Japan

name: Ginza Tsuboyaki-imo
what: Pot-roasted sweet potato specialist using traditional clay-jar method
why: October is the front edge of yakiimo season; closed Mon + 1st/3rd Sundays — Sun Oct 18 closed, open Sun Oct 25

name: Onigiri Asakusa Yadoroku
what: Tokyo's oldest onigiri shop, est. 1954, small counter behind Senso-ji
why: Short walk from base; go early or expect a wait — sells out
mapQuery: Onigiri Asakusa Yadoroku 3-9-10 Asakusa Tokyo Japan

name: Yayoi Kusama Museum
what: Small dedicated museum for Kusama's polka-dot infinity installations
why: REQUIRES advance booking — Oct tickets sold Aug 1; Thu/Fri Oct 22-23 most likely to have stock; 90-min timed slots
mapQuery: Yayoi Kusama Museum 107 Bentencho Shinjuku Tokyo Japan

name: Kamakura
what: Coastal temple town with Daibutsu, Hase-dera, and the Enoden line
why: ~1.5 hrs each way from Asakusa; Enoden running between houses and along the coast is excellent on 120 film — back in Tokyo for dinner
mapQuery: Kamakura Daibutsu Great Buddha Kanagawa Japan

name: Kapital Legs Ebisu
what: The bottoms-only Kapital shop a few minutes from the flagship, in the Ebisu Sunny Building at 2-23-12 Ebisu-minami; said to stock more than a hundred jeans styles.
why: If the goal is to try on every Kapital cut in one afternoon, this is the room to do it in. Walkable with the flagship and Duffle, so the three Ebisu stores are one stop.

name: Kapital Duffle
what: Denim-led lifestyle store at 2-24-2 Ebisu-minami with homewares and original goods, plus exhibitions, workshops and pop-ups.
why: The third Ebisu store and the most different from the other two; check what is on while you are there. Together the three Ebisu shops are the densest Kapital cluster outside Kojima.

name: Kapital SOHO Roppongi
what: Kapital's Roppongi Hills shop, Hill Side 1F at 6-10-1 Roppongi, open 11:00–20:00.
why: Roppongi Hills is ten minutes from Azabudai Hills Sky Lobby and Tokyo Tower, so both Roppongi stores fold into the Tower afternoon instead of needing their own trip.

name: Kapital Legs Roppongi
what: Second Kapital shop inside Roppongi Hills Hill Side, bottoms-focused like its Ebisu namesake.
why: Same building as SOHO Roppongi: two doors in one stop.

name: Kapital Ginza
what: Kapital's Ginza store on the 1st and 3rd floors of the Shimaharu Building, 1-21-12 Ginza, at the Kyobashi end of the district.
why: Ten minutes from Lemon-sha and the yakiimo shop, so it slots into the Ginza half-day; add the two Roppongi doors and that afternoon covers three of the six Tokyo stores.

name: Zojo-ji
what: Head temple of Jodo Buddhism in Tokyo, its main hall framed by Tokyo Tower, with the Tokugawa shogun graves behind; grounds free, about 9:00–17:00.
why: The temple that belongs in the Tower afternoon: it sits between Atago Shrine and Red° Tokyo Tower, and the tower-over-temple frame is the classic shot.

name: Sengaku-ji
what: Soto Zen temple with the graves of the 47 ronin, a small museum and an incense-smoke courtyard; free, roughly 7:00–17:00 in October.
why: Direct on the Asakusa line from the hotel (Sengakuji station), so it is an easy zen-temple hour on any half-empty morning, and pairs with Happo-en garden ten minutes away.

name: Gotoku-ji
what: Soto Zen temple said to be the origin of the maneki-neko, with thousands of white beckoning cats stacked beside the pagoda; grounds free, about 6:00–18:00.
why: The cat temple, three Odakyu stops from Shimokitazawa, so it drops into Tuesday before the SHELTER show; the cat rhyme to Yanaka Ginza.

name: Tsukiji Hongan-ji
what: Jodo Shinshu temple rebuilt in 1934 as an Indian-style stone hall, with a pipe organ inside; free, opens 6:00.
why: Ten minutes from Hamarikyu, so it stacks with the garden on the way to the Yurikamome on Thursday, or with Ginza on Saturday. Unlike any other temple in the city.

name: Yushima Seido
what: Confucian temple of black-lacquered halls in a cedar grove beside Ochanomizu station, with the largest Confucius statue in the world; free, about 9:30–16:00 in October.
why: Two minutes from Kanda Myojin and the music street, so it is a free ten-minute detour on the Monday drum walk.

name: Toyokawa Inari Tokyo Betsuin
what: Soto Zen temple (a temple, despite the torii) crowded with hundreds of stone foxes in red bibs; free, early morning to evening.
why: Ten minutes from Aoyama by the Ginza line at Akasaka-mitsuke; the photogenic zen stop if the Friday Harajuku day wants one non-shopping hour.
mapQuery: Toyokawa Inari Tokyo Betsuin Akasaka Japan

name: Hamarikyu Gardens
what: Edo-period shogunal garden on the bay with a seawater tidal pond, a teahouse on an island and skyscrapers behind; ¥300, 9:00–17:00.
why: It is beside Shiodome, where you change to the Yurikamome, so it is the natural first stop on the Thursday waterfront arc, or the quiet hour before Ginza on Saturday.

name: Rikugien
what: Edo stroll garden of 1702 built around 88 scenes from classical poetry, with hills, a pond and a teahouse; ¥300, 9:00–17:00.
why: Two Yamanote stops from Nippori, so it is the garden that pairs with the Yanaka and Nezu morning. Autumn illumination usually starts late November, so October is daytime only.

name: Koishikawa Korakuen
what: Tokyo's oldest surviving Edo garden (1629), Chinese-influenced, with a full-moon bridge and a miniature Arashiyama; ¥300, 9:00–17:00.
why: Iidabashi is on the Tozai line, so it is a forty-minute detour on the Tuesday west-side run before Nakano; the deepest garden in the city for the least travel.

name: Shinjuku Gyoen
what: Former imperial garden with Japanese, English and French sections and a greenhouse; ¥500, closed Mondays, last entry 16:00 in October.
why: Ten minutes from Sekaido, so Sunday's camera and stamp-book run can end in a garden instead of a crowd; the Japanese garden's teahouse pond is the calm shot of the day.
mapQuery: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden Tokyo Japan

name: Nezu Museum Garden
what: Kengo Kuma's museum of East Asian art with a steep, mossy garden of stone lanterns, teahouses and a pond; museum ticket required, closed Mondays, 10:00–17:00.
why: Five minutes from Momotaro Aoyama and TAIKO-LAB, so the Friday shopping stretch gets a garden in the middle of it; the bamboo entrance corridor alone is worth the ticket.

name: Imperial Palace East Gardens
what: The old Edo Castle inner grounds: massive stone walls, the keep base and the Ninomaru stroll garden; free, closed Mondays and Fridays, gates close 16:30 in October.
why: Ten minutes' walk from Kapital Ginza and Tokyo Station, so it fits the Ginza half-day; the biggest quiet space in central Tokyo, and free.
mapQuery: Imperial Palace East Gardens Tokyo Japan

name: Kyu-Shiba-rikyu Garden
what: Compact Edo daimyo garden around a pond, ringed by office towers; ¥150, 9:00–17:00.
why: Beside Hamamatsucho station, between Zojo-ji and Hamarikyu, so it is a fifteen-minute add-on to either rather than a destination.
mapQuery: Kyu Shiba Rikyu Garden Hamamatsucho Tokyo Japan

name: Happo-en Garden
what: Free stroll garden at a wedding venue, with a centuries-old bonsai collection, a pond and a teahouse serving matcha.
why: Ten minutes from Sengaku-ji, so the two make a quiet Asakusa-line half-morning.

name: Kencho-ji
what: Japan's oldest Zen training monastery (1253) and first of Kamakura's Five Great Zen Temples: vast gate, bell, and a pond garden by Muso Soseki behind the abbot's hall; ¥500, 8:30–16:30.
why: If the zen-garden itch is real, Kamakura has what Tokyo mostly lacks, and this is the head of the list; it turns the Kamakura option into a zen day rather than a beach day.

name: Engaku-ji
what: Rinzai Zen temple climbing a wooded hillside right at Kita-Kamakura station, with a Muso Soseki garden and a famous bell; ¥500, 8:00–16:30.
why: First stop off the train from Tokyo; do it and Kencho-ji before the crowds reach the Daibutsu.

name: Hokoku-ji
what: Small Rinzai Zen temple known for its bamboo grove, a dry rock garden and a teahouse where you drink matcha inside the bamboo; ¥400 plus tea, 9:00–16:00.
why: The Kamakura zen garden that photographs best on film; a short bus ride from Kamakura station.

name: Zuisen-ji
what: Muso Soseki's 1327 rock garden cut into the cliff behind the hall, plus a flower garden; ¥200, 9:00–17:00.
why: The most literal zen rock garden in the Kamakura set, and the quietest; walkable from Hokoku-ji.

name: Meigetsu-in
what: Rinzai Zen temple in Kita-Kamakura with a dry rock garden in front of the main hall and the famous round "window of enlightenment" looking onto the inner garden; ¥500, 9:00–16:00.
why: Ten minutes on foot between Engaku-ji and Kencho-ji, so it costs nothing to add to the zen morning. The inner garden only opens for the June hydrangeas and the late-November leaves, so in October you see it through the window, which is the shot anyway.

name: Jomyo-ji
what: Fifth of the Kamakura Five Great Zen Temples, with a raked dry-landscape garden viewed from the Kisen-an teahouse over a bowl of matcha; ¥100 plus tea, 9:00–16:30.
why: Five minutes from Hokoku-ji, so the bamboo grove and this rock garden are one stop; sitting on the teahouse veranda with the garden in front is the calmest half hour of the day.

name: Hase-dera
what: Hillside temple of the eleven-headed Kannon with a pond garden below and a terrace looking over Yuigahama beach and the bay; ¥400, 8:00–16:30 in October.
why: The water half of the Kamakura day: the sea view from the terrace, the garden ponds, and the Enoden along the coast right after. Five minutes from the Daibutsu at Hase station.

name: Kotoku-in (Great Buddha)
what: The 13-metre bronze Great Buddha of 1252, sitting in the open since its hall was washed away in 1498; ¥300, 8:00–17:00 in October, ¥50 more to step inside it.
why: The one Kamakura stop everyone knows, three Enoden stops from Kamakura station and five minutes from Hase-dera, so it slots into the afternoon without a detour.

name: Wanariya indigo dyeing
what: Casual aizome studio at 1-8-10 Senzoku where you indigo-dye a tenugui (about ¥2,500) or a T-shirt (about ¥3,600) with stencils and wax in roughly 45 minutes; walk-ins taken.
why: The craft that rhymes with the raw-denim track: the same indigo, on your own cloth, ten minutes north of Senso-ji and seven from the TX station. Short enough to drop into any Asakusa morning without booking.

name: Mokuhankan Print Party
what: David Bull's ukiyo-e studio at 1-41-8 Asakusa runs hands-on woodblock printing sessions in English where you print a small design from carved blocks and take it home.
why: The print counterpart to the film cameras and the sketchbooks: paper, pigment, registration, pressure. Five minutes from the hotel. The sessions are popular, so book well ahead.

name: Kakimori and Inkstand
what: Kuramae stationery maker where you build a custom notebook (cover, paper, binding, closure; appointment recommended) and, at Inkstand next door, blend your own fountain-pen ink from 14 pigments in a 105-minute reserved session, about ¥5,500 for the first 35 ml bottle.
why: The stamp-book thread taken seriously: a notebook you specified, and an ink colour nobody else has. Kuramae is a twelve-minute walk south of the hotel and Tokyo's small-maker district, so the walk there is part of it.

name: Shinohara Maruyoshi Furin
what: One of the last two Edo furin makers, in the Satake shopping arcade near Shin-Okachimachi, with two workshops: blow your own glass bell and paint it, or paint a pre-blown one.
why: The sound craft: a hand-blown glass chime whose tone is set by the glass you blew, painted from the inside. One Tsukuba Express stop from Akihabara and one from Asakusa, so it sits on Monday's line home.

name: Ito Inbo hanko carving
what: Hand-carved seal shop founded 1947 where, over 90 to 120 minutes with an interpreter, you carve your own hanko into a twig of cherry or sansho wood and keep it; about ten minutes from the TX station or Iriya.
why: You are collecting stamps all week; this is the one you carve yourself, and it doubles as the signature on every eki-stamp page. Books through the usual experience sites.

name: Amezaiku Ameshin candy sculpting
what: Candy-sculpture studio on Hanakawado, the same block as the hotel, where in a small class you shape a rabbit from hot sugar in the three minutes before it sets, after two practice runs.
why: The one craft that is pure fun for a thirteen-year-old and needs zero travel: it is on your block. The guided version bundles a Nakamise walk and matcha; booking direct is cheaper.

name: Ganso Shokuhin Sample-ya
what: Kappabashi food-replica shop with a 40-minute wax workshop (about ¥3,300, reservation needed, age 6+) where you shape two pieces of tempura and a curl of lettuce by pouring wax into warm water.
why: Kappabashi Kitchen Town is five minutes from the TX station, so this drops in after Monday's lesson. Instruction is in Japanese, which is part of the fun; the wax rippling into lettuce the moment it hits the water is the trick.

name: Itoya Ginza
what: Twelve floors of stationery at 2-7-15 Ginza since 1904: paper by the sheet, fountain pens, inks, notebooks, letterpress and a floor you can have cards printed on; 10:00-20:00.
why: The stationery institution, and it is four minutes from Kapital Ginza and Lemon-sha, so it is an option any time the Saturday Ginza stretch is running. Different from Sekaido (discount art supplies) and Kakimori (make your own): this is the deep browse.

name: The Real McCoy's Tokyo
what: Tokyo flagship at 6-25-8 Jingumae, on the Meiji-dori side of Cat Street between Harajuku and Shibuya; open daily 12:00-20:00. Reproduction A-2 and N-1 flight jackets, Buco motorcycle gear, Joe McCoy workwear and Lot 001 denim, all made in Japan.
why: A must on this trip. The most obsessive reproduction house in Japan: they re-spin the yarn and remake the hardware to match originals, which is the same argument as the raw-denim shops but pointed at military and motorcycle clothing. It sits directly on the walk from the Harajuku denim shops down Cat Street to Shibuya, so it costs no detour at all.
mapQuery: The Real McCoy's Tokyo Jingumae Shibuya

name: Ohya Shobo
what: Antiquarian dealer on Yasukuni-dori since 1882, selling original Edo-period woodblock books, ukiyo-e prints and old hand-coloured maps; 10:00-18:00, closed Sundays and public holidays.
why: The one shop in the book town not to miss: real ukiyo-e you can hold and buy, at prices that start far lower than people expect, right after you have pulled your own print at Mokuhankan. The old maps of Edo are the other reason to go in.

name: Komiyama Shoten
what: Four floors of art dealing on the Jimbocho main street: photobooks on the second floor, fashion magazines, art and design books, posters and prints above and below.
why: The photobook floor is the draw. Japanese photography as objects rather than images, which is the natural companion to buying a film camera at the start of the week.
